name: Dive Deep
definition: Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, audit frequently, and are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ. No task is beneath them.
why: If you do not understand the details of the business, you will fail. Dive Deep is getting to the root cause. Good leaders peel layers. They ask why until they hit something they can fix so it stays fixed. When a senior person does that, the team gets more rigorous, because sloppy stories stop surviving contact with the facts.

Look for skepticism when the metric and the anecdote disagree. Intuition is a starting point. Then you test it. When the data is not sitting in a dashboard, good people go get it. They do not take a deck at face value, and they do not derail a meeting with twelve more cuts that will not change the decision.

Diving deep is how you learn what matters. You demystify the process, the system, and the tool. You find the breaking point before it breaks. You understand a defect well enough to build a fix that scales, not a point patch that comes back next month. That is also how you train {lp:are-right-a-lot}. Judgment without details is a guess you got away with.

It is not micromanagement. Micromanagement is controlling the minutiae and doing the owner's job for them. Dive Deep is understanding the details, then setting audits that keep your hand on the pulse without living in the spreadsheet. You test the assumption, then you step back and let the owner own it. No task is beneath you. That does not mean every task is yours.
calibrationIntro: Score whether someone can get to root cause and then let the owner run. Under accepts the slide. Over lives in the data and never decides. Product-line and unit-economics stories count; jargon does not make the answer deeper.

rows.situation: When reviewing contribution or unit economics
rows.under: Looks at the category total against last year and never drills into product line, supplier, or cost component.
rows.justRight: Reviews the top and bottom product lines on a useful cadence, splits contribution into components (for example, shipping cost), and names both the unit-level actions and the root-cause problem (for example, supplier funding missing on every product from that supplier).
rows.over: Daily analysis of the top 1,000 contributors by every component, with a request for the state of each product. The report takes most of the day and leaves no time to fix anything.

rows.situation: When data is presented in a review
rows.under: Takes every number at face value. Does not ask how it was built, or whether it is agenda-free.
rows.justRight: Challenges how the number was derived, probes outliers, and tests both the data and the presenter's reading of it.
rows.over: Derails the meeting by asking for the same data cut twelve ways, with no story for how the next cut would change the decision.

rows.situation: When a key metric looks wrong
rows.under: Treats the unusual number as weather and waits until the business is already hurt.
rows.justRight: Forms a hypothesis, finds the root cause, and puts a preventative fix in place so the same problem does not return.
rows.over: Spins up a crowd and a week of work for a blip with almost no business impact.

rows.situation: When a program beats the plan
rows.under: Enjoys the good week and learns nothing.
rows.justRight: Studies why it worked, then doubles down and replicates the principle wherever it holds.
rows.over: Spends the win investigating why last year was bad, because that is what made this year look good, and never uses the time to scale what is working.

rows.situation: When the work needs another pair of hands
rows.under: Unwilling to step in. Treats the messy task as beneath them.
rows.justRight: Rolls up sleeves when the owner is stuck, follows through, and then hands the work back.
rows.over: Jumps in at the slightest deviation and stifles ownership and invention.

rows.situation: When staying connected to the work
rows.under: Delegates and only talks to the immediate team.
rows.justRight: Stays connected at every level: walks the floor, talks to people who do the work, and still works through the people who lead them.
rows.over: Works several levels down and changes direction without telling the leaders in between.

rows.under: Treats metrics as a high-level weather report and never learns the drivers.
rows.justRight: Knows the underlying drivers, how they have trended, and who owns each one.
rows.over: Lives in the minutiae, loses the larger picture, and uses the data pile as a substitute for a decision.

rows.under: Fixes the symptom. Always delegates the question. Cannot describe the cause in one sentence.
rows.justRight: Reviews the metrics, asks why until the cause is specific, and then decides.
rows.over: Analysis paralysis. No decision, and no delegation.

rows.situation: When a business case or variance lands on the desk
rows.under: Skips due diligence. Accepts the projection and creates a controllership risk.
rows.justRight: Does enough work to find the blind spots, then improves the proposal so the company is better off.
rows.over: Asks for irrelevant detail, blocks momentum, and micromanages the author.

rows.situation: When making a claim in a room
rows.under: Leads with I think. Blames other teams without data. Stays high-level and fakes fluency.
rows.justRight: Can get to the supporting fact, or to the person who has it, quickly. Calls a detail only when it changes something larger. Does not fake it.
rows.over: Drills every cell with no sense of what matters. Berates people who cannot produce a trivia answer on the spot.

examples.title: When the metric and the story disagree
examples.body: The dashboard is green. Three customers and two operators are telling a different story. The leader does not pick a side. They pull the raw events, walk the path a customer walks, and find the missing filter that made the metric look healthy. Skepticism when metric and anecdote differ is the whole principle in one move.

examples.title: Product-line economics, not a category shrug
examples.body: Contribution for the category looks fine against last year. A weekly pass on the top and bottom product lines shows shipping cost eating the margin on one supplier's entire set, and a funding term that never landed. The action is specific: fix those products, and fix the supplier term so the next set does not arrive broken. A daily census of 1,000 products would have used the week and fixed nothing.

examples.title: Audit, then step back
examples.body: A leader can sit in the data and rebuild the model. They do it once, to learn where the bodies are. Then they put a short audit in place (weekly exceptions, a reconciling check, a walk of the floor) and give the work back to the owner. Doing the owner's job every Tuesday is not Dive Deep. It is a different job, unpaid.

looksLike.individual: An individual who dives deep can explain the system they own in one pass: where the data comes from, where it breaks, who consumes it, and what happens if load goes up by a factor of four. They ask why until the cause is a sentence. They do not fake fluency, and they do not need a week to answer a question they should already know.
looksLike.manager: A manager who dives deep can operate at every level without becoming the bottleneck. They audit. They walk the floor. They know the drivers well enough to catch a bad story in a review. They do not skip the leaders in between, and they do not confuse a pile of cuts with understanding. After they have the fact, they let the owner own the fix.

deepen: Can you state the problem in one sentence, including what should be happening versus what is happening?
When the metric and the anecdote disagree, which one did you follow first, and what did you pull to reconcile them?
Are you solving a symptom, or can you name the cause specifically enough that a fix would stay fixed?
Which number in the last review did you accept without asking how it was built?
If load on your system went up by a factor of four, where does it break first?
What audit do you run so you stay connected to the details without sitting in the owner's chair?
Where is the data you are missing, who has it, and why have you not asked them yet?
Are you treating this as a problem you have already seen, and applying a familiar fix without testing the assumption?
How does this problem show up for the customer, for the team on call, and for the teams upstream and downstream?
What would you stop measuring so you have time to act on the few drivers that move the business?

related.note: Dive Deep is how judgment gets trained. Without the details, being right is luck.
Deep on one-way doors, fast on two-way doors. Endless cuts after you know enough is not rigor.
You cannot raise the bar on a process you do not understand.
No task is beneath an owner. Micromanaging someone else's task is not ownership.
Root cause work that never ships a fix is a research paper.
